title: About
text:
Ada Lovelace, JD PhD
I am a data scientist, university lecturer, and consultant whose work sits at the intersection of applied machine learning, policy research, and education. I think of this practice as poetical science — the conviction that rigour and imagination belong together.

What I do
As Chief Data Scientist at Analytical Engine Data, Ltd. I lead consulting engagements for clients including GlaxoSmithKline, AstraZeneca, the Bank of England, the National Health Service, HM Treasury, the BBC, and Lloyd’s of London. My work spans the full data science lifecycle: gathering requirements, designing scalable models, and deploying solutions that inform real decisions.
As Teaching Professor at the University of Cambridge I teach programming (Python, SQL), statistics, machine learning, and reproducible scientific publishing. I redesigned beginner and intermediate Python curricula and created a new course on reproducible dissemination.


Background
I completed my Ph.D. in Educational Leadership & Policy Analysis at Cambridge, where my research touched on learning measurement, design of experiments, psychometrics, and longitudinal analysis. Before that I earned a Juris Doctor from the University of London — founding a scholarship fundraising programme for LGBT+ law students along the way — and a B.A. in History from Oxford, where I founded Peer Diversity Educators.
Earlier in my career I led data science at UCAS, co-authored grant applications totalling nearly £2 million, and served in research and policy roles at the University of London and the University of Durham.

title: Applied ML for Healthcare Clients
text:
Applied ML for Healthcare Clients
Through Analytical Engine Data, Ltd. I have led engagements for healthcare clients including the National Health Service and major pharmaceutical companies (GlaxoSmithKline, AstraZeneca). Projects span clinical analytics, commercial decision support, and operational optimisation.

Representative work
Predictive modelling for clinical outcomes
Designed and implemented supervised learning models to identify patient cohorts at elevated risk, supporting early intervention programmes. Worked closely with clinical and data engineering teams to ensure model outputs were interpretable and actionable.
NLP and generative AI advisory
Advised clients on practical applications of large language models and natural language processing — including structured data extraction from clinical notes, literature synthesis, and regulatory documentation drafting — with appropriate attention to hallucination risk and audit requirements.
Reproducible analytical pipelines
Developed reproducible data science workflows emphasising stakeholder communication: documented code, version-controlled environments, and plain-language summaries of modelling decisions and limitations for non-technical audiences.


Approach
Healthcare analytics sits in a high-stakes regulatory environment. I design solutions that are robust, explainable, and maintainable — not just accurate. The first deliverable in any engagement is a clear statement of the analytical question; the last is a handoff that the client’s team can own.

Ongoing consulting at Analytical Engine Data, Ltd., Cambridge, 2021–present.

title: MATH 711 — Reproducible Scientific Publishing
text:
MATH 711 — Reproducible Scientific Publishing
I designed and deliver this course at the University of Cambridge for graduate students across quantitative disciplines. It is built on the conviction that the how of publishing — not just the what — is itself a scientific contribution.

What the course covers
Students leave with practical fluency in:

Literate programming — weaving code, prose, and output into a single auditable document (Quarto, R Markdown, Jupyter)
Version control — Git workflows for solo and collaborative research
Reproducible environments — dependency management, containerisation basics, and the principle of the locked environment
Open dissemination — preprint culture, licensing, data sharing norms, and FAIR principles



Design philosophy
The course is deliberately tool-agnostic at the level of values: the point is not to use any particular software but to internalise the habit of reproducibility. Assignments are assessed on whether a stranger can re-run the work from scratch and obtain the same result — not just whether the conclusions are correct.

Taught at the University of Cambridge, MATH 711, from January 2022.

title: Predicting University Applicant Behaviour
text:
Predicting University Applicant Behaviour
During my time at UCAS I built and curated a catalogue of predictive models designed to understand and forecast the behaviour of university applicants across England, Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland.

The problem
University admissions planning depends on knowing not just who applies, but who will accept an offer, enrol, and persist. Without reliable forecasts, institutions over- or under-provision places, accommodation, and support services — at significant cost to students and institutions alike.


Approach
Working from a data warehouse I helped design and implement, I developed models predicting:

Acceptance probability — given an offer, will a candidate accept?
Enrolment probability — given acceptance, will they register on the first day?
Early withdrawal risk — within the first year, which students are most at risk of leaving?

Methods included logistic regression, gradient boosting, and k-nearest neighbours classifiers, with feature engineering drawing on applicant demographics, subject choices, prior attainment, and timing signals. All workflows were implemented in Python with reproducible notebooks.


Outcomes
Models informed UCAS’s institutional intelligence products used by over 400 universities. The underlying research agenda — including randomised controlled trials and quasi-experimental econometric analyses — was supported by grant funding totalling nearly £2M.

Conducted at UCAS (Universities and Colleges Admissions Service), Cheltenham, 2018–2020.

title: Predicting Student Academic Performance
text:
Predicting Student Academic Performance
As Senior Divisional Policy Adviser at the University of London, I developed and introduced a predictive model to forecast student academic performance — one of the first applications of machine learning to student success at the institution.

The problem
Academic risk often goes undetected until a student has already failed an assessment or missed a deadline. By that point, the window for effective early intervention has narrowed considerably. The question was whether structured data available at enrolment and during the first weeks of term could provide reliable early warning signals.


Approach
I drew on administrative records — prior attainment, enrolment patterns, engagement signals, and demographic data — to train a classification model identifying students at elevated risk of underperformance. The feature set was deliberately limited to data already collected in the course of normal university operations, ensuring the model could be maintained without new data infrastructure.
Model outputs were translated into a simple risk tier visible to personal tutors and student support staff, coupled with recommended follow-up protocols — so that the model’s predictions turned into real contact.


Impact
The model was integrated into the institution’s student support workflow. It contributed to the development of subsequent intervention programmes designed to improve retention and student success.

Developed at the University of London, 2017–2018.

text:
Data Governance for a Government Department
At Whitehall Analytics I was embedded with the Office of the Chief Data Officer at a major UK government department to provide expertise on advanced analytics and data governance.

The challenge
Large government departments accumulate data across dozens of legacy systems, with inconsistent standards, unclear ownership, and limited analytical capability. The client needed both strategic direction and practical frameworks to begin building a data-driven culture from within.


What I did

Assessed current state — planned and executed qualitative and quantitative research to understand the department’s data-related capacity, gaps, and needs across business units.
Defined data standards — served as subject-matter expert on data quality, data sharing, and data policy; developed guidance adopted department-wide.
Scoped analytical solutions — gathered and interpreted business requirements to design scalable data science solutions appropriate to a regulatory environment.
Managed delivery — coordinated multiple simultaneous technical workstreams, tracking scope, risk, and dependencies.



Constraints and principles
Government work demands careful attention to data privacy, security classification, and procurement rules. Solutions were designed to be auditable, maintainable by in-house teams, and compliant with relevant frameworks — not optimised for novelty.

Conducted at Whitehall Analytics, London, 2020–2021.
